title: ECS Task Scaling Under SQS Backpressure: Queue Depth Arithmetic, Target Tracking Limits, and the Overshoot Problem
description: How ECS target tracking scaling on SQS queue depth breaks under burst load, and how to design backpressure-aware consumers in Go.
linkedin_post:
ECS autoscaling on SQS queue depth looks simple until a partner dumps 500k events in 90 seconds.

The control loop has real latency: 60s metric evaluation + 60s cooldown floor + Fargate task launch time. That's 2–3 minutes of your existing tasks absorbing the full burst before a single new task is running.

Three things break in that window:

→ Visibility timeout expiry. Messages fetched but not processed in time become visible again, triggering redelivery storms and duplicate processing paths.

→ OOM from unbounded goroutine buffering. If your Go consumer pulls messages before acquiring a semaphore, you've removed them from the visible count without having capacity to process them.

→ Post-scale-out overshoot. The queue drains, scale-in fires before the system stabilizes, another scale-out cycle begins.

The less obvious issue: `ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible` does not include in-flight messages. Under saturation, saturated tasks have already pulled their batch—visible count drops, the scaling signal shows healthy, but workers are buried.

The fix is a composite metric:
effective_depth = ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible + ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible

Scale on that, not the default.

The Go consumer shape matters equally. Gate the ReceiveMessage call behind the semaphore, not just the processing goroutine. Only pull what you have capacity to handle. Use a per-message heartbeat goroutine to extend visibility for long handlers rather than relying on queue timeout.

For extreme burst patterns, pair target tracking with a step-scaling emergency tier at a high depth threshold. The emergency action bypasses metric evaluation latency and adds capacity immediately.

I wrote up the full mechanics: control loop timing, Go consumer implementation, the overshoot cycle, and a concrete decision framework for choosing your scaling configuration.
